title: [Autour de La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois, pages 1 à 67] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context. This page is from the manuscript notes for La Longue Marche (1981). The surrounding pages study sections of the fundamental-group extension. Let S be a henselian trait with fraction field K. Let U = X \ T be a smooth curve over S, and let f_K ∈ U(K) be a rational point with associated section ψ of E_U over K. The previous page states that the following are equivalent:
- (a) f_K extends to a section S → U.
- (b) ψ comes from a section of E_U over E_S.
- (b') ψ, composed into E_U, kills the inertia I ≅ T(\bar K).
The hard direction is (b) ⇒ (a). By descent one reduces to S strictly local. Then X is smooth and proper of relative dimension 1 and genus g, and T is finite étale, so T ≅ I_S is a disjoint union of ν = card I sections g_i, with (g,ν) ≠ (0,1). By properness f extends to a section of X, and one must show that f(S) ⊂ U.

Setup on this page. Argue by contradiction. Suppose f is a section of X/S, distinct from the g_i, which meets g_{i0} at the closed point s. Then Y = S \ {s} = Spec K maps to U, giving π_1(Y) → π_1(U). Grothendieck claims this map is non-trivial when ν ≥ 2. More precisely, its abelianization H_1(Y,Z_ℓ) = T_ℓ(\bar K^*) ≅ Z_ℓ(1) → H_1(U,Z_ℓ) is non-zero for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. This contradicts (b').

Argument. The rational section of the Albanese torsor J^1_{X/S} defined by f is regular, since f extends to X and J^1 is an abelian-scheme torsor (Néron property). So the inertia acts trivially after projection to H_1(J^1_{X/S}) = T_ℓ(Jac). Hence the image of H_1(Y) lies in the toric part ker(H_1(U) → H_1(X)). This toric part is isomorphic to H_1(U_s), the special fibre, and canonically to Z_ℓ(1)^I / Z_ℓ(1) (diagonal): the loops around the cusps modulo the relation that their sum is zero. This is the torus G_m^I/G_m of the generalized Jacobian of U. The toric part vanishes for ν = 1, so the homological criterion fails there; the next page says ν = 1 must be treated separately.

Next page: the computation of the map (11), T_ℓ → T_ℓ^I/T_ℓ. Grothendieck 'guesses' the answer via the intersection multiplicity μ = length V/g_{i0}^*(J_f) of f and g_{i0} at x = g_{i0}(s). The expected (and correct) answer is: the map sends the generator to μ·e_{i0} mod the diagonal. Reason: a local equation t of g_{i0} pulls back under f to an element of valuation μ, so the Kummer class of t∘f is μ times the generator. Since μ ≥ 1, ν ≥ 2 and Z_ℓ(1)^I/diag is torsion-free, the class is non-zero. Hence the inertia acts non-trivially, which gives (b) ⇒ (a) for ν ≥ 2.

The ν = 1 case can be handled by passing to a tame Kummer/étale cover of U that has at least 2 cusps. Such a cover exists unless U is the affine line, which explains the exclusion (g,ν) ≠ (0,1).
errors: The claim is stated for ν ≥ 2 only. The ν = 1 case (toric part zero) is explicitly left open here and needs a non-abelian or covering argument.
The note writes 'T_ℓ^I / T_ℓ' for the toric part; this should be understood as Z_ℓ(1)^I modulo the diagonal. This is correct but stated without proof.
The scribbled marginal 'T_ℓ(\hat R^*)' should be T_ℓ(\bar K^*) ≅ H_1(Y,Z_ℓ). This is the tame inertia of K, not of the ring R.

ideas.what: Criterion: a K-point of an affine curve U extends to an integral point of U iff its associated Galois section is unramified (kills inertia).
ideas.modern_name: Integral points vs unramified sections; local/cuspidal behaviour of the section conjecture
ideas.usually_credited_to: Implicit in Grothendieck's 1983 letter to Faltings; developed by Nakamura, Tamagawa, Mochizuki and Stix (e.g. Stix, Rational points and arithmetic of fundamental groups, 2013)
ideas.where_published: Possibly the typed La Longue Marche (1981) and the letter to Faltings (1983)

ideas.what: Use regularity of the section of the Albanese torsor J^1 (Néron property) to force inertia into the toric part of H_1(U), and identify that part with Z_ℓ(1)^I / Z_ℓ(1).
ideas.modern_name: Weight/toric filtration on H_1 of an open curve; Kummer map of the generalized Jacobian (semi-abelian, Rosenlicht)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard (Deligne's weights; SGA 7 / Grothendieck's monodromy theory)
ideas.where_published: SGA 7 I (toric part, monodromy), in spirit

ideas.what: The inertia image equals intersection multiplicity μ times the loop around the cusp g_{i0} (continued on the next page).
ideas.modern_name: Local Kummer class / intersection pairing with cusps (local height-type computation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore; appears in work on cuspidal sections and local heights

missed.claim: An explicit early (1981) proof sketch that, over a strictly henselian trait, a rational point reducing into a cusp gives a ramified section. The ramification is detected ℓ-adically as μ·e_{i0} in the cusp torus Z_ℓ(1)^I/Z_ℓ(1), with μ the intersection multiplicity. This anticipates the later integral-points/cuspidal-sections theory around the section conjecture, but is close to known folklore.
missed.quote: H_1(Y,Z_ℓ) s'envoie dans la partie torique de H_1(U,Z_ℓ) (← H_1(U_s,Z_ℓ)), qui est canoniquement isomorphe à T_ℓ^I/T_ℓ
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Documents Grothendieck's own route to the integral-point form of the section conjecture, via Néron/Albanese and toric parts; of historical interest only.

deep.surprise_reason: A correct and essentially standard argument (Néron property plus toric part of H_1 plus Kummer theory). It is historically interesting as an early form of the integral-point/ramification criterion for sections, but the mathematics is known.
transcription_corrections: 'T_ℓ(\hat{R}^*)' in the margin is more likely T_ℓ(\bar K^*) (or T_ℓ(\hat K^*)), labelling H_1(Y,Z_ℓ).
'Je dis que est hom. non pas trivial' should read 'Je dis que cet hom. n'est pas trivial'.
'qui est canoniquement isomorphe à 𝕋_ℓ^I/𝕋_ℓ': the symbols are blackboard-bold T_ℓ (i.e. Z_ℓ(1)).
'Soit fixé i_0 ∈ I' is probably 'Soit fixé i_0∈I' / 'fixons i_0∈I'.
